What we learned tracking leads to revenue

A breakdown of the setup, the surprises and the decisions that changed when an HVAC team followed every lead all the way to the invoice.

Savvy Team Growth strategy · Savvy Post Marketing

Published September 30, 2026 · 5 min read

The starting point

This breakdown is a composite of work with established HVAC companies: teams with several trucks, a busy office and a marketing mix of paid search, local service ads, a little social and a lot of word of mouth. Each of them could report on leads. None could reliably report on revenue by source.

The goal was simple to say and fiddly to do: for every booked job, know where the customer first came from and what the job was worth.

The setup

  • Dedicated tracking numbers for each paid channel and for the website.
  • A required lead-source dropdown in the CRM, with no free text.
  • A weekly export joining CRM leads to invoices in the field-service software.
  • One shared definition of a “qualified lead”.

None of this is exotic. The hard part was getting everyone who touched a lead to fill the source the same way, every time.

What surprised us

Volume and value pointed in different directions

The channel that produced the most calls was not the one that produced the most revenue. High-volume channels brought plenty of small repair calls; a quieter channel brought fewer leads that were far more likely to become replacements. Judged on lead count alone, the budget would have moved the wrong way.

Illustrative example: the same month viewed two ways
ChannelShare of leadsShare of booked revenue
Paid searchHighMedium
Local service adsMediumMedium
Referrals & repeatLowHigh
SocialLowLow

The leaks were mostly operational

Once leads were visible end to end, the biggest drop-offs were not in the ads at all. They were missed calls at lunchtime, estimates that never got a second touch, and maintenance customers who were never offered a replacement conversation.

“The first report didn’t change the ads. It changed the phone schedule.”

The decisions it changed

With revenue by source on one page, budget conversations got shorter. Instead of debating impressions, the team could ask which channels produced profitable work and whether there was room to grow them. Spend moved gradually towards the channels that produced larger jobs, and the office added cover for the hours with the most missed calls.

In practice · HVAC

A monthly 30-minute review: revenue by source, missed calls by hour, open estimates older than a week. Three numbers, one owner each.

What we would do differently

Looking back, the setup took longer than it needed to because the team tried to fix every source at once. It would have been faster to start with the two largest paid channels, get them clean, and add the rest one at a time. A partial picture you trust beats a complete picture you don’t.

We would also have agreed the definition of a qualified lead on day one. Without it, the office counted every call, marketing counted only new customers, and the owner counted only jobs over a certain size. The numbers were all correct and none of them matched, which made the first few reviews about arithmetic instead of decisions.

Finally, we would have shared the report with the people answering the phones much earlier. When the office team could see which calls turned into the biggest jobs, they started asking better questions on the first call, and source data improved without anyone being told to try harder.

If you want to try it

  1. Start with the source field. Make it required and limit the options.
  2. Join leads to invoices once a week, even in a spreadsheet.
  3. Review revenue by source monthly and write down one decision each time.

Key takeaways

  • Lead volume and revenue told different stories about the same channels.
  • Clean source data mattered more than clever attribution.
  • The biggest wins came from operations, not ad changes.
  • A monthly revenue-by-source review changed how budget was set.
